title: Security & Compliance: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence Workflows, and Risk Exceptions
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Summary:
This document consolidates Redwood Inference's operating guidance for access control (RBAC and authentication), audit logging, data residency & retention, secure SDLC controls, incident response for security events, compliance evidence workflows, and the risk & exceptions process. It is intended for platform engineers, security reviewers, SREs, and compliance owners who implement or assess controls for Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

Sections:
1) Purpose and scope
- Purpose: Provide prescriptive, auditable controls and operational procedures so security controls are consistently implemented and evidence is producible for audits (ISO/ SOC/ PCI / customer RFPs).
- Scope: All production and customer-facing systems (control plane, serving runtime, telemetry, customer-managed private control planes). Excludes personal development machines except where explicitly required by secure SDLC controls.

2) RBAC & Authentication
Overview:
- Principle of least privilege (PoLP) and role-based access control (RBAC) apply across all Redwood services: Console, Control Plane APIs, Internal Admin UIs, CI systems, and Cloud accounts.
- Authentication: SSO (OIDC/SAML) via corporate identity provider (IdP). Robots/service accounts use short-lived keys + rotation via Vault or KMS integrations.

Roles and ownership:
- Roles: admin, platform-engineer, infra-ops, security-auditor, product-readonly, support-agent (scoped), customer-admin (for private deployments).
- Owner: Security owns RBAC model, Product/Platform own role semantics, Teams own per-service permission mappings.

RBAC policy rules (examples):
- Admin: full access to create/modify deployments and billing actions — limited to <10 individuals and require 2FA and manager approval.
- Platform-engineer: can deploy and manage runtime configs but cannot access customer data unless explicitly authorized via documented escalation.
- Security-auditor: readonly access to logs, audit trails, and compliance evidence buckets.

Implementation checklist:
- All service endpoints use role-to-action mappings in a single source-of-truth (IAM service).
- Policies are codified as YAML and stored in Git (policy repo) with branch protection and mandatory code review.
- Periodic access reviews (quarterly) run by Security; automated reports are emailed to team leads.
- Service accounts use short-lived credentials (<24h) and are tracked in the credential inventory.

3) Audit Logging
Logging requirements:
- All privileged operations, authentication events (success/failure), token creations/revocations, role grants, and data access events must be logged.
- Logs must include: timestamp (UTC), user/service principal, action, target resource, request-id, and outcome.

Retention and integrity:
- Default retention: 365 days hot, 3 years cold (see Data Residency & Retention section for regional variations).
- Logs are written to an append-only store with immutability and signed digests (S3 Object Lock + periodic snapshot + KMS-based signatures).
- Integrity checks: weekly automated SHA-256 checksums validated against signed manifests.

Alerting and monitoring:
- Critical events (multiple failed auths, privilege escalations, export of customer data, creation of high-privilege accounts) must trigger PagerDuty alerts to Security oncall and create a ticket in the incident tracker.
- Aggregation and retention pipelines use the observability stack (centralized ELK/ClickHouse + long-term cold storage in object storage).

4) Data Residency & Retention
Principles:
- Customers may require EU/US/APAC residency for certain workloads. Redwood supports region-specific deployments and explicit residency controls for data-at-rest.
- Retention policies must be enforceable and auditable per workload.

Standard retention matrix (defaults unless overridden by customer contract):
| Data Type | Hot retention | Cold retention | Notes |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Audit logs | 365 days | 3 years | Signed, append-only |
| Customer input payloads | 30 days | 1 year | Default; customer may request shorter/longer in contract |
| Model artifacts (non-customer) | 730 days | 7 years | Versioned in artifact registry |
| Configuration backups | 90 days | 1 year | Encrypted at rest |

Regional controls:
- Data marked as EU-only must be stored on EU regions both for hot and cold tiers. Cross-region replication for DR requires customer approval.
- Data export requests must follow the Data Export Procedure (see related_pages) and be logged as privileged operations.

Data deletion and proof-of-deletion:
- Deletion workflow: raise deletion job -> scheduler performs soft-delete -> physical deletion after retention window -> post-deletion verification recorded in evidence system.
- Proof-of-deletion: generate manifest of deleted object IDs and corresponding storage tombstones; sign with KMS key and store in evidence ledger.

5) Secure SDLC
Core controls:
- Secure code review: All code changes to control plane, runtime, and telemetry must pass static analysis (SAST) and dependency scanning and have at least one security reviewer for high-risk changes.
- CI gating: PRs with failing security checks cannot be merged. Mandatory staging deployment with integration tests that include negative/fuzz tests for API endpoints dealing with authentication/authorization.
- Secrets management: No secrets in source control. Secrets must be injected from Vault/KMS at runtime. Secrets scanning alerts on commit.
- Third-party dependencies: critical/high CVEs must be remediated within 14 days; medium within 30 days. Exceptions must follow risk & exceptions process.

Developer responsibilities:
- Developers must run local linters and unit tests; pipeline runs SAST, dependency-scan, and DAST for public endpoints.
- Security tags: PRs must include 'security-impact: high/medium/low' labels.

Release and change management:
- Release approvals: security review for any change affecting auth, RBAC, or logging.
- Rollout: canary -> phased -> global with rollback plan. All rollouts must include monitoring dashboards and alerting for auth or access anomalies.

6) Incident response — security procedures
Scope and triage:
- All suspected security incidents follow the Security Incident Response Playbook. This section summarizes the typical high-level process for incidents affecting RBAC, audit logs, data residency, or SDLC compromises.

Immediate actions (first 60 minutes):
1. Triage: Confirm scope and impact; capture volatile evidence (memory, network flows) where needed.
2. Containment: Revoke affected tokens, rotate keys, and isolate impacted services or VPCs. Use 'emergency-access' policy to enable fast mitigation with 2-person approval.
3. Notification: PagerDuty alert escalation to Security lead and notify Product/Legal as required by contract.

Forensics and root cause:
- Preserve logs and snapshots to a signed evidence bucket; create a forensics timeline with event correlation IDs.
- Use immutable copies of logs and flow captures. For privileged access incidents, capture the RBAC change history and reviewer approvals.

Post-incident actions (72 hours – 90 days):
- Full postmortem with security classification, impact, timeline, remediation actions, and follow-ups assigned to owners.
- Required changes (e.g., policy hardening, SSO config updates, rotation of all keys) tracked in remediation tracker and verified by Security.
- Notify customers for incidents that meet notification thresholds per contract/regulation.

7) Compliance evidence workflows
Evidence types and storage:
- Evidence artifacts: policy documents, access review logs, signed retention manifests, audit log snapshots, SAST/DAST reports, vulnerability remediation records, incident postmortems, change approvals, and training records.
- Storage: Evidence ledger is an encrypted object store with index metadata in the compliance DB. Each artifact has an immutable identifier, signer, and timestamp.

Requesting and producing evidence:
- Standard requests are handled via the Compliance Portal (internal) and routed to owners. SLA: 5 business days for standard evidence requests, 2 business days for auditor on-site requests.
- Automated evidence exports exist for common audits (ISO/SOC templates) and include signed manifests.

Audit runbook (high level):
1. Intake: Compliance receives scope and timeframe from auditor.
2. Map control families to artifacts and assign owners.
3. Pull artifacts, validate signatures and retention metadata, produce audit package.
4. Deliver package via secure file transfer; log delivery event and receipt.

8) Risk & exceptions process
When to use:
- Exceptions are for documented, short-lived deviations from standard controls (e.g., time-limited elevated access for emergency debugging, delayed patching due to compatibility risk).

Approval workflow:
- Submit exception request in the Risk Tracker (fields: rationale, impacted systems, compensating controls, start/end dates, risk owner).
- Security triages and assigns a risk rating (low/medium/high/critical). High/critical exceptions require Security, Engineering VP, and Legal signoff.
- Approvals have maximum durations: low (90 days), medium (30 days), high (14 days), critical (7 days).

Required compensating controls (examples):
- Timeboxed access with session recording, additional logging retention, multi-person approval for sensitive commands, and automated alerts on anomalous use.

Exception review and closure:
- Weekly exception dashboard for Security and CTO. On expiry, exceptions are either closed (control restored) or escalated for renewal with additional justification.

9) Ownership, metrics, and SLAs
Ownership:
- Security: policy approval, incident playbook, quarterly access review cadence.
- Eng-Platform: RBAC implementation, IAM service, and policy-as-code repo.
- Eng-SRE: logging pipeline, retention enforcement, and integrity verification.
- Legal/Compliance: evidence requests, contractual residency clauses.

Key metrics (examples):
- Mean time to revoke compromised credential: target <= 15 minutes.
- Access review completion rate: target 100% quarterly.
- Evidence request SLA: 95% delivered within 5 business days.
- Log ingestion completeness: >= 99.9% of expected events per day.

10) Appendices
Appendix A — Example RBAC YAML snippet:
---
- role: platform-engineer
  allowed_actions:
    - deploy:runtime
    - view:metrics
    - manage:configs
  constraints:
    - cannot: access:customer-data
---
Appendix B — Incident quick commands (internal)
- Revoke token (CLI): rw-cli auth revoke --token-id <token> --reason "suspected compromise"
- Snapshot logs (CLI): rw-cli logs snapshot --since "2027-03-01T00:00:00Z" --to s3://evidence-ledger/incident-<id>/

Appendix C — Evidence retention mapping (short table):
| Artifact | Hot retention | Cold retention | Owner |
| SAST reports | 365 days | 3 years | Eng-Platform |
| Access reviews | 365 days | 7 years | Security |

Contact and escalation:
- Primary owner: Security (security@redwoodinference.internal)
- Oncall: see Security PagerDuty rota (internal link)
